p.x:
On Saturday, my family went to the circus. We had seats in the front row, so we could see everything!
First, a funny clown came out. He had big shoes and a red nose. Then a magician did some amazing tricks. He made a bird disappear! After that, a beautiful dancer danced on a horse.
In the second part, there was a puppet show for the children. The puppets wore colourful masks. At the end, a famous actress sang a song. I want to go again next year!

Going to the theatre is a special experience. You can choose from many kinds of shows: a musical with songs and dancing, a ballet, an opera, or a serious drama. In Thailand, you can also see khon, a traditional masked dance.
Most people buy tickets online or at the box office. Big shows usually have an interval halfway through, when people buy drinks and snacks. At the end, the audience shows its appreciation with loud applause.
But a lot happens before the first performance. First, the director chooses the actors. To get the lead role, an actor must do well in an audition. Then the cast reads the script and starts to rehearse, often for many weeks. The props, such as swords, letters or crowns, must be ready, and the spotlight must be in the right place.
On the night, actors put on their costumes and make-up in the dressing room. Many, even experienced ones, suffer from stage fright. If something goes wrong, they have to improvise. Some shows are hilarious comedies; others are gripping thrillers. One of the most famous types is the tragedy, and the playwright William Shakespeare wrote many of the best. Some theatres also host circus acts, with an acrobat or a juggler.

Few experiences match the excitement of opening night. Months of preparation lead to the premiere, when critics fill the seats and the cast discovers whether the production will be a success or a flop. For a large musical, dozens of people work behind the scenes: a choreographer designs every dance, technicians control lights and sound, and an usher guides the audience to their seats.
Theatre is live, and anything can happen. Actors forget lines, props break and costumes tear. Experienced performers learn to ad-lib so smoothly that the audience rarely notices. If a lead actor falls ill, an understudy, who has learned the role but rarely performs it, must step in at short notice. Some understudies have become stars after one unexpected night.
The structure of a play is carefully designed to hold attention. Tension builds steadily towards the climax, the moment of greatest drama, before the story is resolved. A powerful monologue, in which a single character speaks their thoughts aloud, can be one of the most memorable moments of a performance.
When a show truly moves its audience, the reaction is unforgettable. At the end, the actors return to the stage for a curtain call, and occasionally the entire audience rises for a standing ovation. Many theatres also offer an afternoon matinee, which is often cheaper and popular with families and older people.
